paragraphs: The last paper completed the observations meant to introduce a fair survey of the plan of government reported by the Convention. We now proceed to carry out that part of our undertaking.

The first question that presents itself is whether the general form and aspect of the government is strictly republican. Plainly, no other form would be reconcilable with the spirit of the people of America, with the fundamental principles of the Revolution, or with the honorable determination, which animates every devotee of liberty, to rest all our political experiments on the capacity of mankind for self-government. So if the plan of the Convention is found to depart from the republican character, its advocates must give it up as no longer defensible.

What, then, are the distinctive characteristics of the republican form? Suppose we sought the answer not by turning to principles but by looking at how political writers have applied the term to the constitutions of different States. We would never find a satisfactory one. Holland, in which not a particle of the supreme authority is derived from the people, has almost universally been called a republic. The same title has been given to Venice, where a small body of hereditary nobles exercises absolute power over the great body of the people in the most absolute manner. Poland, a mixture of aristocracy and monarchy in their worst forms, has been honored with the same name. The government of England has only one republican branch, combined with a hereditary aristocracy and monarchy, and it has with equal impropriety often been placed on the list of republics. These examples are nearly as unlike one another as they are unlike a genuine republic, and they show how extremely inaccurate the use of the term has been in political discussions.

Suppose we look for a standard in the different principles on which different forms of government are founded. We may then define a republic to be, or at least may give that name to, a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior. It is ESSENTIAL to such a government that it be derived from the great body of the society, not from an inconsiderable proportion of it or a favored class within it. Otherwise a handful of tyrannical nobles, exercising their oppressions through a delegation of their powers, might aspire to the rank of republicans and claim for their government the honorable title of republic. It is SUFFICIENT for such a government that the persons who administer it be appointed, either directly or indirectly, by the people, and that they hold their appointments by one of the tenures just specified. Otherwise every government in the United States, and every other popular government that has been or can be well organized or well executed, would be stripped of its republican character. Under the constitution of every State in the Union, some of the officers of government, or other, are appointed only indirectly by the people. Under most of them the chief executive himself is so appointed. Under one, this mode of appointment extends to one of the co-ordinate branches of the legislature. Under all the constitutions, also, the highest offices are held for a definite period, and in many instances, in both the legislative and executive departments, for a period of years. Again, under the provisions of most of the constitutions, as well as according to the most respected and accepted opinions on the subject, the members of the judiciary department are to keep their offices by the firm tenure of good behavior.

When we compare the Constitution planned by the Convention with the standard fixed here, we see at once that it conforms to it in the strictest sense. The House of Representatives, like that of at least one branch of every State legislature, is elected directly by the great body of the people. The Senate, like the present Congress and the Senate of Maryland, derives its appointment indirectly from the people. The President is derived indirectly from the choice of the people, following the example of most of the States. Even the judges, with all the other officers of the Union, will be chosen by the people themselves, though by a remote choice, as in the individual States. The duration of the appointments is equally in accordance with the republican standard and with the model of the State constitutions. The House of Representatives is elected periodically, as in all the States, and for a term of two years, as in the State of South Carolina. The Senate is elected for a term of six years, which is only one year more than the term of the Senate of Maryland and only two more than that of the Senates of New York and Virginia. The President is to continue in office for four years; as against that, in New York and Delaware the chief executive is elected for three years, and in South Carolina for two years. In the other States the election is annual. In several of the States, however, no constitutional provision is made for impeaching the chief executive, and in Delaware and Virginia he cannot be impeached until he is out of office. The President of the United States can be impeached at any time while he remains in office. The tenure by which the judges are to hold their places is, as it unquestionably ought to be, that of good behavior. The tenure of ministerial offices in general will be a matter of legal regulation, in accordance with the reason of the case and the example of the State constitutions.

If any further proof of the republican complexion of this system were required, the most decisive would be found in its absolute prohibition of titles of nobility, under both the federal and the State governments, and in its express guaranty of the republican form to each of the latter.

"But it was not sufficient," say the adversaries of the proposed Constitution, "for the convention to adhere to the republican form. They ought, with equal care, to have preserved the FEDERAL form, which regards the Union as a CONFEDERACY of sovereign states; instead of which, they have framed a NATIONAL government, which regards the Union as a CONSOLIDATION of the States." And it is asked by what authority this bold and radical innovation was undertaken. The use that has been made of this objection requires that we examine it with some precision.

We need not inquire into the accuracy of the distinction on which the objection is founded. To estimate its force justly, we need only do three things. First, we must establish the real character of the government in question. Second, we must inquire how far the Convention was authorized to propose such a government. Third, we must ask how far the duty it owed to its country could make up for any lack of regular authority.

First. To establish the real character of the government, we may consider it in relation to five things: the foundation on which it is to be established; the sources from which its ordinary powers are to be drawn; the operation of those powers; the extent of them; and the authority by which future changes in the government are to be introduced.

Take the first relation. On one hand, it appears that the Constitution is to be founded on the assent and ratification of the people of America, given by deputies elected for the special purpose. On the other hand, this assent and ratification is to be given by the people, not as individuals making up one entire nation, but as making up the distinct and independent States to which they respectively belong. It is to be the assent and ratification of the individual States, derived from the supreme authority in each State, the authority of the people themselves. The act establishing the Constitution will therefore be, not a NATIONAL act, but a FEDERAL act.

That it will be a federal act and not a national one, in the sense these terms have for the objectors, is obvious from one consideration alone. It will be the act of the people as forming so many independent States, not as forming one aggregate nation, because it is to result neither from the decision of a MAJORITY of the people of the Union nor from that of a MAJORITY of the States. It must result from the UNANIMOUS assent of the individual States that are parties to it. It differs from their ordinary assent only in being expressed, not by the legislative authority, but by that of the people themselves. Suppose the people were regarded in this transaction as forming one nation. Then the will of the majority of the whole people of the United States would bind the minority, in the same way that the majority in each State must bind the minority. And the will of the majority would have to be determined either by comparing the individual votes or by taking the will of the majority of the States as evidence of the will of a majority of the people of the United States. Neither of these rules has been adopted. Each State, in ratifying the Constitution, is considered a sovereign body, independent of all others, and bound only by its own voluntary act. In this relation, then, the new Constitution, if established, will be a FEDERAL and not a NATIONAL constitution.

The next relation is to the sources from which the ordinary powers of government are to be derived. The House of Representatives will derive its powers from the people of America, and the people will be represented in the same proportion and on the same principle as in the legislature of a particular State. So far the government is NATIONAL, not FEDERAL. The Senate, on the other hand, will derive its powers from the States, as political and coequal societies, and these will be represented on the principle of equality in the Senate, as they now are in the existing Congress. So far the government is FEDERAL, not NATIONAL. The executive power will be derived from a very compound source. The immediate election of the President is to be made by the States in their political characters. The votes allotted to them follow a compound ratio, which treats them partly as distinct and coequal societies and partly as unequal members of the same society. The eventual election, again, is to be made by that branch of the legislature which consists of the national representatives; but in this particular act they are to be formed into individual delegations from so many distinct and coequal bodies politic. From this aspect the government appears to be of a mixed character, presenting at least as many FEDERAL as NATIONAL features.

The difference between a federal and a national government, as it relates to the OPERATION OF THE GOVERNMENT, is supposed to lie in this. In the former, the powers operate on the political bodies that make up the Confederacy, in their political capacities. In the latter, they operate on the individual citizens who make up the nation, in their individual capacities. When we try the Constitution by this criterion, it falls under the NATIONAL, not the FEDERAL character, though perhaps not so completely as has been understood. In several cases, and particularly in the trial of controversies to which States may be parties, the States must be viewed and proceeded against only in their collective and political capacities. So far, on this side, the national countenance of the government seems to be disfigured by a few federal features. But this blemish is perhaps unavoidable in any plan. The operation of the government on the people in their individual capacities, in its ordinary and most essential proceedings, may on the whole entitle it, in this relation, to be called a NATIONAL government.

But if the government is national with regard to the OPERATION of its powers, it changes its aspect again when we consider it in relation to the EXTENT of its powers. The idea of a national government involves not only an authority over the individual citizens but an unlimited supremacy over all persons and things, so far as they are objects of lawful government. Among a people consolidated into one nation, this supremacy is vested completely in the national legislature. Among communities united for particular purposes, it is vested partly in the general legislature and partly in the municipal legislatures. In the former case, all local authorities are subordinate to the supreme authority, and it may control, direct or abolish them at pleasure. In the latter case, the local or municipal authorities form distinct and independent portions of the supremacy, and within their respective spheres they are no more subject to the general authority than the general authority is subject to them within its own sphere. In this relation, then, the proposed government cannot be considered a NATIONAL one, since its jurisdiction extends only to certain enumerated objects and leaves to the individual States a residuary and inviolable sovereignty over all other objects. It is true that in controversies about the boundary between the two jurisdictions, the court that is ultimately to decide is to be established under the general government. But this does not change the principle of the case. The decision is to be made impartially, according to the rules of the Constitution, and all the usual and most effective precautions are taken to secure this impartiality. Some such court is clearly essential to prevent an appeal to the sword and a dissolution of the compact. That it ought to be established under the general government rather than under the local governments, or, to speak more properly, that it could safely be established under the first alone, is a position not likely to be disputed.

If we try the Constitution by its last relation, to the authority by which amendments are to be made, we find it neither wholly NATIONAL nor wholly FEDERAL. If it were wholly national, the supreme and ultimate authority would reside in the MAJORITY of the people of the Union, and this authority would be competent at all times, like that of a majority of every national society, to alter or abolish its established government. If it were wholly federal, on the other hand, the concurrence of every State in the Union would be essential to any alteration that would bind all. The mode provided by the plan of the Convention is not founded on either of these principles. In requiring more than a majority, and particularly in computing the proportion by STATES, not by CITIZENS, it departs from the NATIONAL character and moves toward the FEDERAL. In making the concurrence of less than the whole number of States sufficient, it loses the FEDERAL character again and shares in the NATIONAL.

The proposed Constitution, therefore, is in strictness neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both. In its foundation it is federal, not national. In the sources from which the ordinary powers of the government are drawn, it is partly federal and partly national. In the operation of these powers it is national, not federal. In their extent, again, it is federal, not national. And finally, in the authoritative mode of introducing amendments, it is neither wholly federal nor wholly national.
